description: Be a viewer of the cooking show or participate in it.

english.UI_CONTRACT_POTATO_DESC:
Good morning, 47.

Today, your destination is Viñedo Yates - a winery on the outskirts of Mendoza, Argentina, where a major culinary TV show is being filmed, produced by the top brass of the Russian mafia. A double contract awaits you there.

Your targets are Michael «Mickey» Moravitz, an ambitious Czech-born British chef who gained worldwide fame after winning a celebrity TV show and opening his own restaurant, and Martin Vergopoulos, a cold and rational food critic, famous for his enigmatic, emotionless public image.

One of our clients recently conducted a private investigation into Moravitz that lasted several years - and was able to find substantial evidence of Michael's involvement in the death of one of the icons of US rap music. After arriving in Britain to undergo an expensive heroin rehabilitation program, he visited Moravitz's restaurant before entering the treatment, where he ordered an expensive dish from the restaurant's elite menu. A few days later, while undergoing detoxification from opiates, the artist died - the cause of death was attributed to the presence of narcotics in his blood, despite the fact that the rapper had long been warned of all the risks and, by all accounts, was completely clean. Due to lack of evidence, no investigation was opened; however, our client - the manager and close friend of the deceased - was able to link the murder to the restaurant and confirm the presence of opium in some of its exclusive dishes - after which he filed a contract.

As for Vergopoulos - the controversial Greek-American critic - the contract for his assassination is in no way connected to the first client. Our second client is a high-ranking FSB official who wished to remain anonymous. Having close ties to the leadership of Russian organized crime groups, influenced by them, he decided to become one of the main producers of a cooking show sponsored by Roman Khabko - a notorious Russian crime lord. 
However, our client recently learned some highly controversial information about the filming: Michael Moravitz, the chef we've already become familiar with, who leads one of the cooking teams, is in cahoots with the show's judge, Martin Vergopoulos. 

Our client wants to avoid a scandal that could erupt if news of the fraud leaked outside the show. He fears that his ties to the Russian mafia will be exposed if rumors spread, possibly leading to an investigation or action by Khabko, so he urgently needs to disrupt the filming and eliminate everyone who knows about the cheating in order to remain in the shadows of the canceled show and conceal his affiliation with criminal groups.

Soon you'll find yourself at Viñedo Yates itself, attending the show as a live audience member - but be careful. During the TV production, the winery will be under much tighter security than usual - including Khabko's personal security guards from the «Siberian Tigers», who are there to ensure their leader's safety and make sure the filming goes off without a hitch.

Still, don't think I'm worried, Agent - you know what to do.

Good luck, 47.
english.actor_wtl_desc:
Michal Moravitz was born in 1997 in Ostrava, Czech Republic. He was the only child of a factory worker and a seamstress, whose financial situation was far from ideal: due to the economic crisis in the country, most steel plants were shut down - including the one where the head of the family, Michal's father, worked. On top of that, the devastating floods raging across Central Europe at the time threatened the well-being of a family that was already in a tight spot. Shortly after Michal turned one, the family decided to leave Czechia and migrate west in search of financial security - they ended up choosing the United Kingdom. 

After moving to London, the family struggled but managed to settle into their new home quickly. His father found a job in metalworking - but his salary was still barely enough to support the family, which forced his mother to take a job as a cook at a local budget hotel.
Having spent most of his early childhood in the kitchen - since his mother had to take him to work with her, unable to leave the child home alone for long - he developed an interest in cooking that eventually grew into a passionate obsession. He was fascinated by the freedom and flexibility of cooking - his mother often told him how she used techniques from Czech traditional cuisine to enrich British desserts and dishes, which she often found too plain and dull - and Moravitz sincerely admired her enthusiasm and experimental approach to cooking, which became the main reason he went on to connect his life with the culinary arts, often mentioning memories of his mother in his cookbooks and during interviews.

Michal spent his late childhood and teenage years in a very diverse environment - ever since preschool, as he tried to integrate into local life, he never had any trouble learning English, which he considered his native language - it was easy for him to fit into an English-speaking environment, and soon most of his acquaintances knew him not as Michal, but as Mickey - it became a sort of nickname for him, which eventually evolved into a middle name outside the home. However, he was never able to completely shake off the impacts of immigration. As he lived in a part of the city predominantly populated by refugees of low socioeconomic status, making English friends proved to be much harder than he had imagined. Most of his neighbors were immigrants from Afghanistan who had come to Britain under a government refugee resettlement program. 

With a social circle consisting of people from the lower strata of London society, he quickly became involved with unsavory circles - and from there, he was introduced quite early to tobacco, alcohol, and even drugs - in particular opium and its derivatives - such as heroin, which was incredibly popular among the local marginalized population.
As he grew older, Moravitz's school performance and relationship with his father slowly deteriorated - not because he didn't understand the material, but because he didn't feel he wanted to devote time to his studies - his life at that point consisted mainly of scraping by on breadcrumbs, surviving on the family's meager savings, and his hard life instilled in him determination and ambition - but along with that, arrogance and selfishness. Gradually, he began to look down on his father, seeing him as a foolish and stubborn failure who had spent his entire life doing backbreaking work for pennies - he, on the other hand, desired a completely different fate for himself and was ready to do practically anything to become successful, while putting in as little unnecessary effort as possible. 

His thirst for profit led young Mickey to associate with even more shady figures - an Afghan crime syndicate that controlled a significant portion of the drug trafficking in the area where he lived. Ever since childhood, he had known several boys from school who were connected to the group: it was they who helped him find a job in the city as a drug courier after several months of working for free for the organization as a driver.
But even so, Moravitz didn't particularly enjoy being an errand boy - at first, it seemed like a step up, but with his ambitious nature, he very quickly grew bored with the job, which began to seem lousy to him - yet with his charisma, silver tongue, and ability to take the initiative, he quickly forged even stronger ties within the clan and was «promoted» to an independent street dealer.

But his desire for profit gradually grew into something bigger - working as a dealer, Mickey was already making enough to move out of his parents' house and live a much better life than before - but by that point, he felt as if even that wasn't enough for him anymore. He needed something more - he realized he was capable of more than just a «normal» life: the «moderate prosperity» he had always strived for now seemed boring and mediocre to him - social connections, career advancement, and other minor successes, especially compared to his parents', gave Mickey reason to believe he was above the «gray masses» - that he had the right to think bigger than most people. He needed fame and recognition.
Moravitz found his chance to make it big on a culinary show that, after a long break, had begun accepting applicants again - for him, this was not only an opportunity to show what he was capable of, but also a path to dedicating his life to what brought him joy: cooking. 

To him, this chance seemed practically one in a million - but among the hundreds of other applicants for the show, it was very easy to miss out on this opportunity, which Moravitz couldn't afford to do - so he decided to use his syndicate's head's connections in show business - he asked his boss to put in a good word for him so he'd be accepted onto the show - and in return, he promised to repay him somehow.
Soon after, Mickey also officially changed his name to Michael Moravitz, but he still continued to call himself Mickey most of the time.

After making it onto the show, he immediately won over both the hosts and the audience - his combination of charisma, witty, sharp humor, and arrogant confidence in his own victory - combined with bold culinary choices that blended elements of Czech, British, and Middle Eastern cuisines - opened up a world of opportunities for him to impress and spark interest.
In addition to honest play, he also sought victory through other means - sometimes even sabotaging other contestants' cooking, spoiling ingredients and equipment, or spreading rumors about them that would make their presence on the show undesirable.
As the project progressed, the organizers came to realize more and more that keeping Moravitz on set was extremely beneficial - he was in his element in front of the cameras and moved through the kitchen like a fish in water. By the end of filming, he had practically become the face of the season - his triumph was guaranteed.

The prize for winning the show was the opportunity to open his own restaurant in the centre of London with funding from the show - and Michael certainly took advantage of it, founding the restaurant «Morava», which specializes in Czech folk cuisine and dishes similar to those Moravitz prepared on the show.
The restaurant was an instant commercial success, catapulting it to media fame and making its owner, Mickey, one of Britain's most famous chefs.
However, the time soon came for the star to repay his debt to the clan leader - and Michael kept his word, allowing the restaurant to be used as a logistics hub for storing and distributing the clan's opiates under one simple condition: not to tarnish his image or interfere with the kitchen's operations.

But despite the restaurant's wild popularity, its owner felt, as always, that something was still missing - in search of a special, unique gastronomic experiences that Moravitz wanted to link not only to the spectrum of taste but also to the emotional register, he decided to use an additional ingredient with which he was personally very familiar - opium.
Michael considered the «exclusive menu» he had developed - available to VIP clients for exorbitant sums of money - to be his greatest achievement. For him, it wasn't just about food - he wasn't simply trying to make sure people liked the taste. He wanted his dishes to be a complete, unforgettable experience for the customer - one that would make them feel something they had never felt before and would never feel again. 
Diners, unaware of all the details behind the preparation of these exclusive dishes, truly developed a deep affection for his culinary masterpieces, unable to unravel the mystery of such vivid sensations from a simple meal.

Soon, new horizons opened up for Mickey to develop his public image: after a visit from Nikolai Kamarov, an influential FSB official and political figure from the Kremlin with ties to the Russian mafia, who described the dishes from the special «Morava» menu as the finest culinary experience of his life, Moravitz's name became extremely popular among the upper echelons of the Russian mafia, which also opened up many new opportunities for him. He was recently invited to film a new cooking show in Argentina, produced by Roman Khabko, one of the most influential Russian criminal «fixers» and Kamarov's close personal friend and business partner. On the show, Moravitz will have to assemble a team of chefs from his restaurant and compete against another team in preparing delicacies for the judges. 

For Mickey, this isn't just another show.
He sees the opportunity to become the favorite chef of Russian crime bosses and to get close to the cream of the criminal underworld of the former USSR as his next goal - one that will take him to a new level in the game - after which he'll truly be able to live the high life, earning hundreds of times more money and influence under the protection of a massive criminal syndicate - which is precisely why he has stooped even lower than usual this time, intending not only to impress the judges with his «special» recipes but also to ensure the complete loyalty of at least one of them - Martin Vergopoulos - by deciding in advance to bribe him and significantly increase his chances of winning. 

However, the finale of this show will turn out quite differently for Moravitz.

english.judge_desc:
The Vergopoulos family emigrated to the United States from Kalavrita after Greece was liberated by Allied forces at the end of World War II. At the time of their relocation, a significant number of family members already had military experience - while living in their hometown, most of the adult men in the family had, in one way or another, been partisans in the anti-fascist resistance, fighting against the Italo-German occupation.

After immigrating, this fact shaped the family's destiny, as many of its members enlisted in the U.S. military. The family's military tradition has endured from the 1950s to the present day.

However, Martin Vergopoulos, born two generations later in Savannah, Georgia, had refused to accept his «destiny» as a soldier - a notion his relatives had instilled in him throughout his life - ever since childhood. Martin's father was Konstantin Vergopoulos - a local politician and member of the Savannah City Council who built his political career through the military, having served as a brigadier general in the U.S. Army: Konstantin spent his entire life in the armed forces and achieved all his success and influence solely - as he believes - through his military career.

His strict and cold father managed to raise Martin to be an extremely disciplined and calm person, but he was never able to quell his son's interest in the arts: Throughout his childhood, despite his family's disapproval, Martin secretly explored various forms of self-expression - music, drawing… He was best at composing and writing texts, but unfortunately for Martin, he held absolutely no interest in such a career.
When Konstantin decided to take on the task of re-educating his son (who, interestingly, was already a teenager at the time) with the goal of immersing him in the basics of military life, Martin was forced to grow closer to the rest of the family. Although he was the eldest among his two newborn twin sisters and his younger brother Lucas, Vergopoulos had always been something of a recluse, interacting little and reluctantly with his relatives, preferring to spend time alone and focus on himself. 

However, this forced closeness with his relatives unexpectedly opened up new horizons for him - as he attended family gatherings more often, he began to pay increasing attention to the dishes - not so much to their taste as to their structure, texture, and various cooking methods. From that moment on, he felt he had discovered a new passion: cooking. Soon he became interested in the culinary process itself - the behind-the-scenes world of gastronomy - and, to the surprise of the entire family, grew closest of all to his mother. Greek cuisine amazed young Martin with its diversity and richness - he became more and more passionate about it with each passing day, trying to devote every spare moment to improving his cooking skills. Despite his unprecedented success in cooking - which his passionate interest, discipline, and determination brought him relatively quickly - his father was only annoyed by his son's new interest. 

Martin spent his final years with his family in a very tense atmosphere - his father regularly took his frustrations out on him, unable to persuade his son to dedicate himself to the «worthy» and «noble» military profession. Just as Martin was finally beginning to grow closer to his sisters and his brother, Konstantin did everything in his power to limit their contact; as a result, upon turning 18, the eldest son decided to leave the family and live on his own. However, a new obstacle arises & his father refused to give Martin the savings the family had set aside for his education, arguing that he «wouldn't know how to manage them». After lengthy arguments, his mother, without his father's knowledge, emptied the savings account and gave the entire sum to Martin, after which he bid farewell to everyone except his father and moved to the town of Hyde Park, in New York State, where, using his savings, he enrolled in the Culinary Institute of America, one of the world's leading culinary colleges.
Over the course of three years at the institute, Martin significantly improved his cooking skills. He was already a fairly good cook before enrolling, having learned to prepare food at home, but the institute opened up a world of new opportunities and recipes for him - as a result, upon graduating, he became one of the top students in his class. In addition, while studying at the institute, he met Finn Flanery - a young, energetic, and ambitious man from Ireland who was studying culinary business management there. They were quickly brought together by a shared dream: to open a restaurant. The modest and calm Chef Vergopoulos quickly became friends with the charismatic entrepreneur Flanery, and after graduating, they moved back to Martin's hometown, Savannah. Renting a modest apartment together, they began planning their next steps.
By putting together the money they both had left and receiving a small investment from Finn's relatives, they managed to open their own Greek restaurant - «Meteora».

Thanks to Flanery's skillful marketing and Vergopoulos' talent, the restaurant quickly became a sensation among locals - it was still a fairly small, homey place that didn't claim to be an upscale establishment, but it was precisely the warm atmosphere and the owners' love for their project that brought «Meteora» its initial success. However, a year after the breakthrough, Vergopoulo's father suddenly reappeared; unwilling to accept that he had been wrong, he was determined to prove to his son that cooking was not a worthy profession. Using his political connections and influence in the city administration - as a member of the city council - he did everything he could to sabotage Martin's business: he falsified tax returns, creating major problems for «Meteora», and set overly nitpicky fire and health inspectors on the restaurant, who always deliberately found something to criticize, even when there was no need. 

These events became a huge source of stress for both Martin and Finn, ultimately leading to disagreements between them - Flannery was angry at Martin because his family was causing problems the restaurant didn't deserve, while Martin, due to the tension, became cold and distant. Later, the business began to suffer serious financial losses due to constant inspections, fines, and tax reassessments - Finn began to feel that meeting Vergopoulos had been his biggest mistake. Soon, «Meteora» closed due to management disputes and financial losses. The two owners, now deep in debt, had a serious dispute, and one day Flanery left their shared apartment for several days without taking his belongings. Soon after, Martin was informed that Finn had died in a motorcycle accident while driving under the influence of alcohol.

The once-popular chef now felt a deep disgust for cooking - as he would say in later interviews, «Every time I had to cook, it took me back to that kitchen - it put me right next to Finn, who, as always, was looking over my shoulder with approval». It was extremely difficult for Martin to come to terms with the guilt he felt over what had happened to Finn.
He was visibly devastated by the loss of a close friend and was not happy about the media attention that Flanery's death had brought. News agencies very quickly picked up on the story of the «sudden death of a bankrupt entrepreneur», but Martin realized that this news story might be his only chance to climb out of the hole he found himself in.  

Forced to capitalize on the tragedy involving Finn, Vergopoulos began giving interviews, telling their story, and sharing details with journalists, soon turning the incident into one of the most high-profile culinary news stories in the U.S. and the U.K. Martin skillfully used his newfound popularity to build a new career as a restaurant critic. The scandalous story, which now always loomed over him, made him an extremely well-known and intriguing figure in the world of culinary critics - especially when combined with his cold and grim demeanor.
 As a sought-after restaurant critic, Martin began earning enough to start climbing out of debt. With every review and every interview, his image became increasingly interesting, and his popularity grew all the faster.

After several years of diligently working on his image, he managed to scrape together enough money to pay off his debts and go into business for himself - though, by his own choice, he set aside a significant portion of his income for the regular compensation payments to Finn's family in Ireland. Because of this, his lifestyle could hardly be called luxurious - taking the payments into account, he earned enough to live well, but relatively modestly. As Martin's popularity grew, new opportunities opened up for him. In addition to various reality shows, competitions, and other familiar events, other, more unusual prospects became available to him.

A few months ago, Vergopoulos received an offer from Roman Khabko, a crime lord with close ties to the Russian mafia. Khabko demanded that Martin write a scathing review of the trendy Los Angeles restaurant «Champagne» - a new establishment opened by one of his old criminal rivals. In return, Khabko promised a handsome sum of money and protection from possible retaliation by the restaurant's owners. Martin, however, politely declined.
Some time later, the situation changed dramatically: Vergopoulos learned that his brother, Lucas - whom he hadn't seen in over twenty years - had been arrested for deserting from the army and was to be prosecuted to the full extent of the law. 
After briefly analyzing what had happened, Martin also learned that his father, disappointed by Lucas's actions, had refused to provide him with legal assistance. 

After a couple of days of reflection, Martin decides to take matters into his own hands and agrees to Khabko's deal, covering the initial legal costs - but this turns out to be insufficient. After half a year of diligently searching for additional income, Khabko approaches Martin again - this time with an offer to serve as a judge on an episode of a cooking show that he sponsors. There, Vergopoulos' responsibility will be to judge the dishes prepared by two teams - a young, innovative culinary art group from Southeast Asia, and the internationally renowned team from the restaurant «Morava».

Martin was familiar with the second team - almost everyone had heard of Mickey Moravitz, the owner and chef of the restaurant. Still, Vergopoulos diligently avoided visiting «Morava» and any interaction with Moravitz due to alarming rumors circulating in the tight-knit circles of the culinary elite about Michael, despite his impeccable public image. On top of that, Martin harbored a certain dislike for Moravitz personally - he didn't like his arrogance and the image he carefully cultivated around himself. His rare and brief encounters with the chef only reinforced his negative impression of him - he turned out to be charismatic, but he was also extremely self-centered, which put Martin off a bit. Unlike Michael, he was more down-to-earth and didn't treat food as something sacred - in Vergopoulos' opinion, food should first and foremost be presentable, properly prepared, pleasant in texture, and, most importantly, delicious. 

When he saw the offer to participate in a show sponsored by the Russian criminal underworld, Martin had no choice but to accept, even though under any other circumstances he would have avoided the notorious chef from «Morava» at all costs.
Still, the payment for the shoot would cover more than half of his remaining legal fees. The day of the trial was approaching, and the critic was desperately looking for more ways to make a quick buck before filming began - but help came from where he least expected it. Mickey Moravitz wasn't stupid - he knew how Vergopoulos felt about him. Michael considered himself good enough to win the show and sincerely believed that his food was the best Martin would ever taste in his life, but still, he couldn't let personal feelings get in the way of his victory.
 Moravitz offered Martin a bribe in exchange for his vote.

Vergopoulos, in fact, had no intention of criticizing the «Morava» team simply because of his personal feelings toward their leader. He had no intention of lowering his scores and was genuinely prepared to give an honest evaluation. But Mickey didn't know that. Forcing himself to go against his principles, Martin was left with no choice but to accept the money to ensure his brother would receive proper legal representation.

This decision would change his life forever.
english.actor_producer_desc:
Little is known about Roman Khabko's early life, but according to some sources, he is the son of a Ukrainian smuggler who illegally shipped gasoline and was killed by Soviet security forces in the early '80s. Khabko is most likely not his real name, but a pseudonym he adopted in the late 1980s while working as a bouncer for one of the leaders of the Russian mafia in New York, where he moved shortly after his father's death.

In New York, Khabko quickly gained a reputation as a brutal thug and rose high in the ranks of the Russian mafia's American branch. He served time in New York prisons on several occasions and then left the country after a drug deal fell through, leaving four dead agents from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration at the scene of the crime.

Upon returning to Russia, Khabko turned to human trafficking: he sold young men and women to oligarchs and high-profile figures visiting the country on business - including, in part, top FSB officials. Very soon, he began working for the country's most influential people - diplomats, successful businessmen, and high-ranking politicians from Russia.

However, when he got carried away and decided to blackmail a foreign diplomat, the Russian authorities immediately intervened and arrested Khabko. He was sent to the remote private «Perm-14» prison, where he spent the last 10 years and eventually became the second-in-command after the prison warden, who was often absent. While in prison, having gained even more power and connections, Khabko began to expand his influence over the market in the Perm Region in the western foothills of the Urals, where he was serving his sentence. By meddling in the trade of a region that produced impressive quantities of oil, gas, potash, and rock salt, he was able to amass a substantial fortune - all while operating through the prison warden, Reznikov, who also received his cut from the schemes.

By that point, a massive scandal had erupted around the «Perm-14» prison. The UN and human rights organizations were shocked by reports of systematic brutality and unpunished murders at the prison, which had become commonplace there due to harsh prison hazing practices and strong ties to criminal organizations.
Around the same time, Khabko - who had already made a substantial fortune by taking advantage of Perm's economy - was planning to secure his own early release by offering Reznikov, the prison warden, an exceptionally large bribe. Khabko probably took this step because he realized that the scandal surrounding the violence at «Perm-14» would likely lead to an investigation and a change in leadership, which he considered undesirable.

Upon learning of the deal, the leadership of the Federal Penitentiary Service of the Russian Federation - which is responsible for overseeing prison conditions - became concerned that if Khabko, a crime boss known for his political connections, were to suddenly be released from prison, it would only fuel the UN's discontent - which is why one of the FSIN leadership members decided to appeal to the ICA to eliminate Khabko and Reznikov in order to hush up the scandal. Agent 47 successfully fulfilled the contract - and soon, news of Reznikov and Khabko's deaths amid the prison riot quickly died down, as did global discontent with the Russian Federal Penitentiary Service.

For about a year and a half, Khabko was presumed dead. However, information later leaked online about an internal FSB investigation indicating that, a few hours before his «death», officers of the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation secretly transported Khabko out of the «Perm-14» complex in a government armored personnel carrier, replacing him with a decoy. It was this impersonator who was later killed during the ICA contract and identified by the security services as Roman Khabko. According to published reports, someone from the FSB leadership was also involved in the escape, though no specific suspects were named.
After details of the escape came to light, the ICA leadership attempted to contact the person who had ordered Roman's original murder - that very individual from the Federal Penitentiary Service - to reopen the contract. However, it quickly became apparent that he had been declared missing shortly after Khabko's escape, so the contract was terminated.

According to some unconfirmed reports, during the time Roman was believed to be dead, he spent his time hiding in Mexico or Colombia under the protection of influential friends and partners linked to South American cartels - in particular, the Delgado crime family. Khabko met the family's former head, Fernando Delgado, while trafficking drugs in the U.S. in the late '90s. After news of his escape broke, Roman - fearing he would be placed on an international wanted list - declared himself a victim of political persecution: he claimed that Russian intelligence agencies had persecuted and imprisoned him purely for political reasons based on his national origin, and that all previous charges against him were fabricated and politically motivated. According to his statements, the escape was a desperate attempt to save himself from a politically driven murder attempt by the Russian government - as evidence, he cited the death of his impersonator shortly after his disappearance from Russia.

After that, Khabko returned to the United States, where he was arrested upon crossing the border on an old charge of murdering four Drug Enforcement Administration agents. However, Roman did not remain in custody for long. He took the initiative to cooperate with the U.S. National Security Council - which was in their best interest. For the Council, Khabko was a gold mine - with his reputation as a victim of political persecution who had fled Russia to save his life, he was an excellent asset and a convenient puppet for diplomatic manipulation. After the deal was signed, Khabko became a political activist whom the U.S. used to discredit the Russian government - and in return, Roman had all previous charges against him dropped and was granted faster access to U.S. citizenship.

Since then, Khabko has lived a lavish lifestyle. With the money he had accumulated, he bought a huge mansion in Los Angeles (where he officially resides), opened dozens of restaurants across the United States, and owns real estate in Colombia - including a villa in Bogotá, the country's capital - as well as smaller properties (mainly warehouses and small manufacturing facilities) located in Barranquilla, Colombia's main port and commercial hub; Cali, a key southern trade and logistics center; and other smaller cities. In addition, he invested in the construction of Rico Delgado's (the new head of the Delgado cartel) mansion in Santa Fortuna, which once again raises questions about his ties to South American organized crime. 

Private investigations were also frequently launched against Khabko's properties and businesses, and charges were brought - for example, his restaurants were accused of money laundering, his Colombian businesses were accused of drug production with cartel support and using slave labor, and Roman himself was accused of making threats and causing physical harm to competitors in the restaurant business. However, these investigations are often quickly closed and then meticulously covered up, and the charges are dropped almost immediately - especially after the U.S. government intervenes on his behalf.

Recently, Khabko took another step toward expanding his business empire by launching his own cooking TV show, the first episode of which will soon begin filming in Argentina. The project's producers also include individuals with ties to Colombian cartels, Perm oil and gas magnates, and, interestingly, people linked to the FSB.
Thanks to a large-scale advertising campaign, the TV show has already captured the interest of viewers around the world - the first episode will feature renowned chef Michael «Mickey» Moravitz and his restaurant team, as well as a promising culinary art group from Southeast Asia. In addition, renowned restaurant critic Martin Vergopoulos was invited to serve as one of the judges, which only fueled the buzz surrounding the show.

However, despite Khabko's financial success, a new contract - unrelated to the previous one - was opened on him a few days ago. This time, it was assigned to Agent Stone. The client is an influential FSB officer who wished to remain anonymous - but we have reason to believe that he is the one linked to the initial escape from «Perm-14» and is attempting, through murder, to cover his tracks and divert suspicion related to the Russian intelligence services continuing investigation of the escape.

french.actor_wtl_desc:
Michal Moravitz was born in 1997 in Ostrava, Czech Republic. He was the only child of a factory worker and a seamstress, whose financial situation was far from ideal: due to the economic crisis in the country, most steel plants were shut down - including the one where the head of the family, Michal's father, worked. On top of that, the devastating floods raging across Central Europe at the time threatened the well-being of a family that was already in a tight spot. Shortly after Michal turned one, the family decided to leave Czechia and migrate west in search of financial security - they ended up choosing the United Kingdom. 

After moving to London, the family struggled but managed to settle into their new home quickly. His father found a job in metalworking - but his salary was still barely enough to support the family, which forced his mother to take a job as a cook at a local budget hotel.
Having spent most of his early childhood in the kitchen - since his mother had to take him to work with her, unable to leave the child home alone for long - he developed an interest in cooking that eventually grew into a passionate obsession. He was fascinated by the freedom and flexibility of cooking - his mother often told him how she used techniques from Czech traditional cuisine to enrich British desserts and dishes, which she often found too plain and dull - and Moravitz sincerely admired her enthusiasm and experimental approach to cooking, which became the main reason he went on to connect his life with the culinary arts, often mentioning memories of his mother in his cookbooks and during interviews.

Michal spent his late childhood and teenage years in a very diverse environment - ever since preschool, as he tried to integrate into local life, he never had any trouble learning English, which he considered his native language - it was easy for him to fit into an English-speaking environment, and soon most of his acquaintances knew him not as Michal, but as Mickey - it became a sort of nickname for him, which eventually evolved into a middle name outside the home. However, he was never able to completely shake off the impacts of immigration. As he lived in a part of the city predominantly populated by refugees of low socioeconomic status, making English friends proved to be much harder than he had imagined. Most of his neighbors were immigrants from Afghanistan who had come to Britain under a government refugee resettlement program. 

With a social circle consisting of people from the lower strata of London society, he quickly became involved with unsavory circles - and from there, he was introduced quite early to tobacco, alcohol, and even drugs - in particular opium and its derivatives - such as heroin, which was incredibly popular among the local marginalized population.
As he grew older, Moravitz's school performance and relationship with his father slowly deteriorated - not because he didn't understand the material, but because he didn't feel he wanted to devote time to his studies - his life at that point consisted mainly of scraping by on breadcrumbs, surviving on the family's meager savings, and his hard life instilled in him determination and ambition - but along with that, arrogance and selfishness. Gradually, he began to look down on his father, seeing him as a foolish and stubborn failure who had spent his entire life doing backbreaking work for pennies - he, on the other hand, desired a completely different fate for himself and was ready to do practically anything to become successful, while putting in as little unnecessary effort as possible. 

His thirst for profit led young Mickey to associate with even more shady figures - an Afghan crime syndicate that controlled a significant portion of the drug trafficking in the area where he lived. Ever since childhood, he had known several boys from school who were connected to the group: it was they who helped him find a job in the city as a drug courier after several months of working for free for the organization as a driver.
But even so, Moravitz didn't particularly enjoy being an errand boy - at first, it seemed like a step up, but with his ambitious nature, he very quickly grew bored with the job, which began to seem lousy to him - yet with his charisma, silver tongue, and ability to take the initiative, he quickly forged even stronger ties within the clan and was «promoted» to an independent street dealer.

But his desire for profit gradually grew into something bigger - working as a dealer, Mickey was already making enough to move out of his parents' house and live a much better life than before - but by that point, he felt as if even that wasn't enough for him anymore. He needed something more - he realized he was capable of more than just a «normal» life: the «moderate prosperity» he had always strived for now seemed boring and mediocre to him - social connections, career advancement, and other minor successes, especially compared to his parents', gave Mickey reason to believe he was above the «gray masses» - that he had the right to think bigger than most people. He needed fame and recognition.
Moravitz found his chance to make it big on a culinary show that, after a long break, had begun accepting applicants again - for him, this was not only an opportunity to show what he was capable of, but also a path to dedicating his life to what brought him joy: cooking. 

To him, this chance seemed practically one in a million - but among the hundreds of other applicants for the show, it was very easy to miss out on this opportunity, which Moravitz couldn't afford to do - so he decided to use his syndicate's head's connections in show business - he asked his boss to put in a good word for him so he'd be accepted onto the show - and in return, he promised to repay him somehow.
Soon after, Mickey also officially changed his name to Michael Moravitz, but he still continued to call himself Mickey most of the time.

After making it onto the show, he immediately won over both the hosts and the audience - his combination of charisma, witty, sharp humor, and arrogant confidence in his own victory - combined with bold culinary choices that blended elements of Czech, British, and Middle Eastern cuisines - opened up a world of opportunities for him to impress and spark interest.
In addition to honest play, he also sought victory through other means - sometimes even sabotaging other contestants' cooking, spoiling ingredients and equipment, or spreading rumors about them that would make their presence on the show undesirable.
As the project progressed, the organizers came to realize more and more that keeping Moravitz on set was extremely beneficial - he was in his element in front of the cameras and moved through the kitchen like a fish in water. By the end of filming, he had practically become the face of the season - his triumph was guaranteed.

The prize for winning the show was the opportunity to open his own restaurant in the centre of London with funding from the show - and Michael certainly took advantage of it, founding the restaurant «Morava», which specializes in Czech folk cuisine and dishes similar to those Moravitz prepared on the show.
The restaurant was an instant commercial success, catapulting it to media fame and making its owner, Mickey, one of Britain's most famous chefs.
However, the time soon came for the star to repay his debt to the clan leader - and Michael kept his word, allowing the restaurant to be used as a logistics hub for storing and distributing the clan's opiates under one simple condition: not to tarnish his image or interfere with the kitchen's operations.

But despite the restaurant's wild popularity, its owner felt, as always, that something was still missing - in search of a special, unique gastronomic experiences that Moravitz wanted to link not only to the spectrum of taste but also to the emotional register, he decided to use an additional ingredient with which he was personally very familiar - opium.
Michael considered the «exclusive menu» he had developed - available to VIP clients for exorbitant sums of money - to be his greatest achievement. For him, it wasn't just about food - he wasn't simply trying to make sure people liked the taste. He wanted his dishes to be a complete, unforgettable experience for the customer - one that would make them feel something they had never felt before and would never feel again. 
Diners, unaware of all the details behind the preparation of these exclusive dishes, truly developed a deep affection for his culinary masterpieces, unable to unravel the mystery of such vivid sensations from a simple meal.

Soon, new horizons opened up for Mickey to develop his public image: after a visit from Nikolai Kamarov, an influential FSB official and political figure from the Kremlin with ties to the Russian mafia, who described the dishes from the special «Morava» menu as the finest culinary experience of his life, Moravitz's name became extremely popular among the upper echelons of the Russian mafia, which also opened up many new opportunities for him. He was recently invited to film a new cooking show in Argentina, produced by Roman Khabko, one of the most influential Russian criminal «fixers» and Kamarov's close personal friend and business partner. On the show, Moravitz will have to assemble a team of chefs from his restaurant and compete against another team in preparing delicacies for the judges. 

For Mickey, this isn't just another show.
He sees the opportunity to become the favorite chef of Russian crime bosses and to get close to the cream of the criminal underworld of the former USSR as his next goal - one that will take him to a new level in the game - after which he'll truly be able to live the high life, earning hundreds of times more money and influence under the protection of a massive criminal syndicate - which is precisely why he has stooped even lower than usual this time, intending not only to impress the judges with his «special» recipes but also to ensure the complete loyalty of at least one of them - Martin Vergopoulos - by deciding in advance to bribe him and significantly increase his chances of winning. 

However, the finale of this show will turn out quite differently for Moravitz.

french.judge_desc:
The Vergopoulos family emigrated to the United States from Kalavrita after Greece was liberated by Allied forces at the end of World War II. At the time of their relocation, a significant number of family members already had military experience - while living in their hometown, most of the adult men in the family had, in one way or another, been partisans in the anti-fascist resistance, fighting against the Italo-German occupation.

After immigrating, this fact shaped the family's destiny, as many of its members enlisted in the U.S. military. The family's military tradition has endured from the 1950s to the present day.

However, Martin Vergopoulos, born two generations later in Savannah, Georgia, had refused to accept his «destiny» as a soldier - a notion his relatives had instilled in him throughout his life - ever since childhood. Martin's father was Konstantin Vergopoulos - a local politician and member of the Savannah City Council who built his political career through the military, having served as a brigadier general in the U.S. Army: Konstantin spent his entire life in the armed forces and achieved all his success and influence solely - as he believes - through his military career.

His strict and cold father managed to raise Martin to be an extremely disciplined and calm person, but he was never able to quell his son's interest in the arts: Throughout his childhood, despite his family's disapproval, Martin secretly explored various forms of self-expression - music, drawing… He was best at composing and writing texts, but unfortunately for Martin, he held absolutely no interest in such a career.
When Konstantin decided to take on the task of re-educating his son (who, interestingly, was already a teenager at the time) with the goal of immersing him in the basics of military life, Martin was forced to grow closer to the rest of the family. Although he was the eldest among his two newborn twin sisters and his younger brother Lucas, Vergopoulos had always been something of a recluse, interacting little and reluctantly with his relatives, preferring to spend time alone and focus on himself. 

However, this forced closeness with his relatives unexpectedly opened up new horizons for him - as he attended family gatherings more often, he began to pay increasing attention to the dishes - not so much to their taste as to their structure, texture, and various cooking methods. From that moment on, he felt he had discovered a new passion: cooking. Soon he became interested in the culinary process itself - the behind-the-scenes world of gastronomy - and, to the surprise of the entire family, grew closest of all to his mother. Greek cuisine amazed young Martin with its diversity and richness - he became more and more passionate about it with each passing day, trying to devote every spare moment to improving his cooking skills. Despite his unprecedented success in cooking - which his passionate interest, discipline, and determination brought him relatively quickly - his father was only annoyed by his son's new interest. 

Martin spent his final years with his family in a very tense atmosphere - his father regularly took his frustrations out on him, unable to persuade his son to dedicate himself to the «worthy» and «noble» military profession. Just as Martin was finally beginning to grow closer to his sisters and his brother, Konstantin did everything in his power to limit their contact; as a result, upon turning 18, the eldest son decided to leave the family and live on his own. However, a new obstacle arises & his father refused to give Martin the savings the family had set aside for his education, arguing that he «wouldn't know how to manage them». After lengthy arguments, his mother, without his father's knowledge, emptied the savings account and gave the entire sum to Martin, after which he bid farewell to everyone except his father and moved to the town of Hyde Park, in New York State, where, using his savings, he enrolled in the Culinary Institute of America, one of the world's leading culinary colleges.
Over the course of three years at the institute, Martin significantly improved his cooking skills. He was already a fairly good cook before enrolling, having learned to prepare food at home, but the institute opened up a world of new opportunities and recipes for him - as a result, upon graduating, he became one of the top students in his class. In addition, while studying at the institute, he met Finn Flanery - a young, energetic, and ambitious man from Ireland who was studying culinary business management there. They were quickly brought together by a shared dream: to open a restaurant. The modest and calm Chef Vergopoulos quickly became friends with the charismatic entrepreneur Flanery, and after graduating, they moved back to Martin's hometown, Savannah. Renting a modest apartment together, they began planning their next steps.
By putting together the money they both had left and receiving a small investment from Finn's relatives, they managed to open their own Greek restaurant - «Meteora».

Thanks to Flanery's skillful marketing and Vergopoulos' talent, the restaurant quickly became a sensation among locals - it was still a fairly small, homey place that didn't claim to be an upscale establishment, but it was precisely the warm atmosphere and the owners' love for their project that brought «Meteora» its initial success. However, a year after the breakthrough, Vergopoulo's father suddenly reappeared; unwilling to accept that he had been wrong, he was determined to prove to his son that cooking was not a worthy profession. Using his political connections and influence in the city administration - as a member of the city council - he did everything he could to sabotage Martin's business: he falsified tax returns, creating major problems for «Meteora», and set overly nitpicky fire and health inspectors on the restaurant, who always deliberately found something to criticize, even when there was no need. 

These events became a huge source of stress for both Martin and Finn, ultimately leading to disagreements between them - Flannery was angry at Martin because his family was causing problems the restaurant didn't deserve, while Martin, due to the tension, became cold and distant. Later, the business began to suffer serious financial losses due to constant inspections, fines, and tax reassessments - Finn began to feel that meeting Vergopoulos had been his biggest mistake. Soon, «Meteora» closed due to management disputes and financial losses. The two owners, now deep in debt, had a serious dispute, and one day Flanery left their shared apartment for several days without taking his belongings. Soon after, Martin was informed that Finn had died in a motorcycle accident while driving under the influence of alcohol.

The once-popular chef now felt a deep disgust for cooking - as he would say in later interviews, «Every time I had to cook, it took me back to that kitchen - it put me right next to Finn, who, as always, was looking over my shoulder with approval». It was extremely difficult for Martin to come to terms with the guilt he felt over what had happened to Finn.
He was visibly devastated by the loss of a close friend and was not happy about the media attention that Flanery's death had brought. News agencies very quickly picked up on the story of the «sudden death of a bankrupt entrepreneur», but Martin realized that this news story might be his only chance to climb out of the hole he found himself in.  

Forced to capitalize on the tragedy involving Finn, Vergopoulos began giving interviews, telling their story, and sharing details with journalists, soon turning the incident into one of the most high-profile culinary news stories in the U.S. and the U.K. Martin skillfully used his newfound popularity to build a new career as a restaurant critic. The scandalous story, which now always loomed over him, made him an extremely well-known and intriguing figure in the world of culinary critics - especially when combined with his cold and grim demeanor.
 As a sought-after restaurant critic, Martin began earning enough to start climbing out of debt. With every review and every interview, his image became increasingly interesting, and his popularity grew all the faster.

After several years of diligently working on his image, he managed to scrape together enough money to pay off his debts and go into business for himself - though, by his own choice, he set aside a significant portion of his income for the regular compensation payments to Finn's family in Ireland. Because of this, his lifestyle could hardly be called luxurious - taking the payments into account, he earned enough to live well, but relatively modestly. As Martin's popularity grew, new opportunities opened up for him. In addition to various reality shows, competitions, and other familiar events, other, more unusual prospects became available to him.

A few months ago, Vergopoulos received an offer from Roman Khabko, a crime lord with close ties to the Russian mafia. Khabko demanded that Martin write a scathing review of the trendy Los Angeles restaurant «Champagne» - a new establishment opened by one of his old criminal rivals. In return, Khabko promised a handsome sum of money and protection from possible retaliation by the restaurant's owners. Martin, however, politely declined.
Some time later, the situation changed dramatically: Vergopoulos learned that his brother, Lucas - whom he hadn't seen in over twenty years - had been arrested for deserting from the army and was to be prosecuted to the full extent of the law. 
After briefly analyzing what had happened, Martin also learned that his father, disappointed by Lucas's actions, had refused to provide him with legal assistance. 

After a couple of days of reflection, Martin decides to take matters into his own hands and agrees to Khabko's deal, covering the initial legal costs - but this turns out to be insufficient. After half a year of diligently searching for additional income, Khabko approaches Martin again - this time with an offer to serve as a judge on an episode of a cooking show that he sponsors. There, Vergopoulos' responsibility will be to judge the dishes prepared by two teams - a young, innovative culinary art group from Southeast Asia, and the internationally renowned team from the restaurant «Morava».

Martin was familiar with the second team - almost everyone had heard of Mickey Moravitz, the owner and chef of the restaurant. Still, Vergopoulos diligently avoided visiting «Morava» and any interaction with Moravitz due to alarming rumors circulating in the tight-knit circles of the culinary elite about Michael, despite his impeccable public image. On top of that, Martin harbored a certain dislike for Moravitz personally - he didn't like his arrogance and the image he carefully cultivated around himself. His rare and brief encounters with the chef only reinforced his negative impression of him - he turned out to be charismatic, but he was also extremely self-centered, which put Martin off a bit. Unlike Michael, he was more down-to-earth and didn't treat food as something sacred - in Vergopoulos' opinion, food should first and foremost be presentable, properly prepared, pleasant in texture, and, most importantly, delicious. 

When he saw the offer to participate in a show sponsored by the Russian criminal underworld, Martin had no choice but to accept, even though under any other circumstances he would have avoided the notorious chef from «Morava» at all costs.
Still, the payment for the shoot would cover more than half of his remaining legal fees. The day of the trial was approaching, and the critic was desperately looking for more ways to make a quick buck before filming began - but help came from where he least expected it. Mickey Moravitz wasn't stupid - he knew how Vergopoulos felt about him. Michael considered himself good enough to win the show and sincerely believed that his food was the best Martin would ever taste in his life, but still, he couldn't let personal feelings get in the way of his victory.
 Moravitz offered Martin a bribe in exchange for his vote.

Vergopoulos, in fact, had no intention of criticizing the «Morava» team simply because of his personal feelings toward their leader. He had no intention of lowering his scores and was genuinely prepared to give an honest evaluation. But Mickey didn't know that. Forcing himself to go against his principles, Martin was left with no choice but to accept the money to ensure his brother would receive proper legal representation.

This decision would change his life forever.
french.actor_producer_desc:
Little is known about Roman Khabko's early life, but according to some sources, he is the son of a Ukrainian smuggler who illegally shipped gasoline and was killed by Soviet security forces in the early '80s. Khabko is most likely not his real name, but a pseudonym he adopted in the late 1980s while working as a bouncer for one of the leaders of the Russian mafia in New York, where he moved shortly after his father's death.

In New York, Khabko quickly gained a reputation as a brutal thug and rose high in the ranks of the Russian mafia's American branch. He served time in New York prisons on several occasions and then left the country after a drug deal fell through, leaving four dead agents from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration at the scene of the crime.

Upon returning to Russia, Khabko turned to human trafficking: he sold young men and women to oligarchs and high-profile figures visiting the country on business - including, in part, top FSB officials. Very soon, he began working for the country's most influential people - diplomats, successful businessmen, and high-ranking politicians from Russia.

However, when he got carried away and decided to blackmail a foreign diplomat, the Russian authorities immediately intervened and arrested Khabko. He was sent to the remote private «Perm-14» prison, where he spent the last 10 years and eventually became the second-in-command after the prison warden, who was often absent. While in prison, having gained even more power and connections, Khabko began to expand his influence over the market in the Perm Region in the western foothills of the Urals, where he was serving his sentence. By meddling in the trade of a region that produced impressive quantities of oil, gas, potash, and rock salt, he was able to amass a substantial fortune - all while operating through the prison warden, Reznikov, who also received his cut from the schemes.

By that point, a massive scandal had erupted around the «Perm-14» prison. The UN and human rights organizations were shocked by reports of systematic brutality and unpunished murders at the prison, which had become commonplace there due to harsh prison hazing practices and strong ties to criminal organizations.
Around the same time, Khabko - who had already made a substantial fortune by taking advantage of Perm's economy - was planning to secure his own early release by offering Reznikov, the prison warden, an exceptionally large bribe. Khabko probably took this step because he realized that the scandal surrounding the violence at «Perm-14» would likely lead to an investigation and a change in leadership, which he considered undesirable.

Upon learning of the deal, the leadership of the Federal Penitentiary Service of the Russian Federation - which is responsible for overseeing prison conditions - became concerned that if Khabko, a crime boss known for his political connections, were to suddenly be released from prison, it would only fuel the UN's discontent - which is why one of the FSIN leadership members decided to appeal to the ICA to eliminate Khabko and Reznikov in order to hush up the scandal. Agent 47 successfully fulfilled the contract - and soon, news of Reznikov and Khabko's deaths amid the prison riot quickly died down, as did global discontent with the Russian Federal Penitentiary Service.

For about a year and a half, Khabko was presumed dead. However, information later leaked online about an internal FSB investigation indicating that, a few hours before his «death», officers of the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation secretly transported Khabko out of the «Perm-14» complex in a government armored personnel carrier, replacing him with a decoy. It was this impersonator who was later killed during the ICA contract and identified by the security services as Roman Khabko. According to published reports, someone from the FSB leadership was also involved in the escape, though no specific suspects were named.
After details of the escape came to light, the ICA leadership attempted to contact the person who had ordered Roman's original murder - that very individual from the Federal Penitentiary Service - to reopen the contract. However, it quickly became apparent that he had been declared missing shortly after Khabko's escape, so the contract was terminated.

According to some unconfirmed reports, during the time Roman was believed to be dead, he spent his time hiding in Mexico or Colombia under the protection of influential friends and partners linked to South American cartels - in particular, the Delgado crime family. Khabko met the family's former head, Fernando Delgado, while trafficking drugs in the U.S. in the late '90s. After news of his escape broke, Roman - fearing he would be placed on an international wanted list - declared himself a victim of political persecution: he claimed that Russian intelligence agencies had persecuted and imprisoned him purely for political reasons based on his national origin, and that all previous charges against him were fabricated and politically motivated. According to his statements, the escape was a desperate attempt to save himself from a politically driven murder attempt by the Russian government - as evidence, he cited the death of his impersonator shortly after his disappearance from Russia.

After that, Khabko returned to the United States, where he was arrested upon crossing the border on an old charge of murdering four Drug Enforcement Administration agents. However, Roman did not remain in custody for long. He took the initiative to cooperate with the U.S. National Security Council - which was in their best interest. For the Council, Khabko was a gold mine - with his reputation as a victim of political persecution who had fled Russia to save his life, he was an excellent asset and a convenient puppet for diplomatic manipulation. After the deal was signed, Khabko became a political activist whom the U.S. used to discredit the Russian government - and in return, Roman had all previous charges against him dropped and was granted faster access to U.S. citizenship.

Since then, Khabko has lived a lavish lifestyle. With the money he had accumulated, he bought a huge mansion in Los Angeles (where he officially resides), opened dozens of restaurants across the United States, and owns real estate in Colombia - including a villa in Bogotá, the country's capital - as well as smaller properties (mainly warehouses and small manufacturing facilities) located in Barranquilla, Colombia's main port and commercial hub; Cali, a key southern trade and logistics center; and other smaller cities. In addition, he invested in the construction of Rico Delgado's (the new head of the Delgado cartel) mansion in Santa Fortuna, which once again raises questions about his ties to South American organized crime. 

Private investigations were also frequently launched against Khabko's properties and businesses, and charges were brought - for example, his restaurants were accused of money laundering, his Colombian businesses were accused of drug production with cartel support and using slave labor, and Roman himself was accused of making threats and causing physical harm to competitors in the restaurant business. However, these investigations are often quickly closed and then meticulously covered up, and the charges are dropped almost immediately - especially after the U.S. government intervenes on his behalf.

Recently, Khabko took another step toward expanding his business empire by launching his own cooking TV show, the first episode of which will soon begin filming in Argentina. The project's producers also include individuals with ties to Colombian cartels, Perm oil and gas magnates, and, interestingly, people linked to the FSB.
Thanks to a large-scale advertising campaign, the TV show has already captured the interest of viewers around the world - the first episode will feature renowned chef Michael «Mickey» Moravitz and his restaurant team, as well as a promising culinary art group from Southeast Asia. In addition, renowned restaurant critic Martin Vergopoulos was invited to serve as one of the judges, which only fueled the buzz surrounding the show.

However, despite Khabko's financial success, a new contract - unrelated to the previous one - was opened on him a few days ago. This time, it was assigned to Agent Stone. The client is an influential FSB officer who wished to remain anonymous - but we have reason to believe that he is the one linked to the initial escape from «Perm-14» and is attempting, through murder, to cover his tracks and divert suspicion related to the Russian intelligence services continuing investigation of the escape.

italian.actor_wtl_desc:
Michal Moravitz was born in 1997 in Ostrava, Czech Republic. He was the only child of a factory worker and a seamstress, whose financial situation was far from ideal: due to the economic crisis in the country, most steel plants were shut down - including the one where the head of the family, Michal's father, worked. On top of that, the devastating floods raging across Central Europe at the time threatened the well-being of a family that was already in a tight spot. Shortly after Michal turned one, the family decided to leave Czechia and migrate west in search of financial security - they ended up choosing the United Kingdom. 

After moving to London, the family struggled but managed to settle into their new home quickly. His father found a job in metalworking - but his salary was still barely enough to support the family, which forced his mother to take a job as a cook at a local budget hotel.
Having spent most of his early childhood in the kitchen - since his mother had to take him to work with her, unable to leave the child home alone for long - he developed an interest in cooking that eventually grew into a passionate obsession. He was fascinated by the freedom and flexibility of cooking - his mother often told him how she used techniques from Czech traditional cuisine to enrich British desserts and dishes, which she often found too plain and dull - and Moravitz sincerely admired her enthusiasm and experimental approach to cooking, which became the main reason he went on to connect his life with the culinary arts, often mentioning memories of his mother in his cookbooks and during interviews.

Michal spent his late childhood and teenage years in a very diverse environment - ever since preschool, as he tried to integrate into local life, he never had any trouble learning English, which he considered his native language - it was easy for him to fit into an English-speaking environment, and soon most of his acquaintances knew him not as Michal, but as Mickey - it became a sort of nickname for him, which eventually evolved into a middle name outside the home. However, he was never able to completely shake off the impacts of immigration. As he lived in a part of the city predominantly populated by refugees of low socioeconomic status, making English friends proved to be much harder than he had imagined. Most of his neighbors were immigrants from Afghanistan who had come to Britain under a government refugee resettlement program. 

With a social circle consisting of people from the lower strata of London society, he quickly became involved with unsavory circles - and from there, he was introduced quite early to tobacco, alcohol, and even drugs - in particular opium and its derivatives - such as heroin, which was incredibly popular among the local marginalized population.
As he grew older, Moravitz's school performance and relationship with his father slowly deteriorated - not because he didn't understand the material, but because he didn't feel he wanted to devote time to his studies - his life at that point consisted mainly of scraping by on breadcrumbs, surviving on the family's meager savings, and his hard life instilled in him determination and ambition - but along with that, arrogance and selfishness. Gradually, he began to look down on his father, seeing him as a foolish and stubborn failure who had spent his entire life doing backbreaking work for pennies - he, on the other hand, desired a completely different fate for himself and was ready to do practically anything to become successful, while putting in as little unnecessary effort as possible. 

His thirst for profit led young Mickey to associate with even more shady figures - an Afghan crime syndicate that controlled a significant portion of the drug trafficking in the area where he lived. Ever since childhood, he had known several boys from school who were connected to the group: it was they who helped him find a job in the city as a drug courier after several months of working for free for the organization as a driver.
But even so, Moravitz didn't particularly enjoy being an errand boy - at first, it seemed like a step up, but with his ambitious nature, he very quickly grew bored with the job, which began to seem lousy to him - yet with his charisma, silver tongue, and ability to take the initiative, he quickly forged even stronger ties within the clan and was «promoted» to an independent street dealer.

But his desire for profit gradually grew into something bigger - working as a dealer, Mickey was already making enough to move out of his parents' house and live a much better life than before - but by that point, he felt as if even that wasn't enough for him anymore. He needed something more - he realized he was capable of more than just a «normal» life: the «moderate prosperity» he had always strived for now seemed boring and mediocre to him - social connections, career advancement, and other minor successes, especially compared to his parents', gave Mickey reason to believe he was above the «gray masses» - that he had the right to think bigger than most people. He needed fame and recognition.
Moravitz found his chance to make it big on a culinary show that, after a long break, had begun accepting applicants again - for him, this was not only an opportunity to show what he was capable of, but also a path to dedicating his life to what brought him joy: cooking. 

To him, this chance seemed practically one in a million - but among the hundreds of other applicants for the show, it was very easy to miss out on this opportunity, which Moravitz couldn't afford to do - so he decided to use his syndicate's head's connections in show business - he asked his boss to put in a good word for him so he'd be accepted onto the show - and in return, he promised to repay him somehow.
Soon after, Mickey also officially changed his name to Michael Moravitz, but he still continued to call himself Mickey most of the time.

After making it onto the show, he immediately won over both the hosts and the audience - his combination of charisma, witty, sharp humor, and arrogant confidence in his own victory - combined with bold culinary choices that blended elements of Czech, British, and Middle Eastern cuisines - opened up a world of opportunities for him to impress and spark interest.
In addition to honest play, he also sought victory through other means - sometimes even sabotaging other contestants' cooking, spoiling ingredients and equipment, or spreading rumors about them that would make their presence on the show undesirable.
As the project progressed, the organizers came to realize more and more that keeping Moravitz on set was extremely beneficial - he was in his element in front of the cameras and moved through the kitchen like a fish in water. By the end of filming, he had practically become the face of the season - his triumph was guaranteed.

The prize for winning the show was the opportunity to open his own restaurant in the centre of London with funding from the show - and Michael certainly took advantage of it, founding the restaurant «Morava», which specializes in Czech folk cuisine and dishes similar to those Moravitz prepared on the show.
The restaurant was an instant commercial success, catapulting it to media fame and making its owner, Mickey, one of Britain's most famous chefs.
However, the time soon came for the star to repay his debt to the clan leader - and Michael kept his word, allowing the restaurant to be used as a logistics hub for storing and distributing the clan's opiates under one simple condition: not to tarnish his image or interfere with the kitchen's operations.

But despite the restaurant's wild popularity, its owner felt, as always, that something was still missing - in search of a special, unique gastronomic experiences that Moravitz wanted to link not only to the spectrum of taste but also to the emotional register, he decided to use an additional ingredient with which he was personally very familiar - opium.
Michael considered the «exclusive menu» he had developed - available to VIP clients for exorbitant sums of money - to be his greatest achievement. For him, it wasn't just about food - he wasn't simply trying to make sure people liked the taste. He wanted his dishes to be a complete, unforgettable experience for the customer - one that would make them feel something they had never felt before and would never feel again. 
Diners, unaware of all the details behind the preparation of these exclusive dishes, truly developed a deep affection for his culinary masterpieces, unable to unravel the mystery of such vivid sensations from a simple meal.

Soon, new horizons opened up for Mickey to develop his public image: after a visit from Nikolai Kamarov, an influential FSB official and political figure from the Kremlin with ties to the Russian mafia, who described the dishes from the special «Morava» menu as the finest culinary experience of his life, Moravitz's name became extremely popular among the upper echelons of the Russian mafia, which also opened up many new opportunities for him. He was recently invited to film a new cooking show in Argentina, produced by Roman Khabko, one of the most influential Russian criminal «fixers» and Kamarov's close personal friend and business partner. On the show, Moravitz will have to assemble a team of chefs from his restaurant and compete against another team in preparing delicacies for the judges. 

For Mickey, this isn't just another show.
He sees the opportunity to become the favorite chef of Russian crime bosses and to get close to the cream of the criminal underworld of the former USSR as his next goal - one that will take him to a new level in the game - after which he'll truly be able to live the high life, earning hundreds of times more money and influence under the protection of a massive criminal syndicate - which is precisely why he has stooped even lower than usual this time, intending not only to impress the judges with his «special» recipes but also to ensure the complete loyalty of at least one of them - Martin Vergopoulos - by deciding in advance to bribe him and significantly increase his chances of winning. 

However, the finale of this show will turn out quite differently for Moravitz.
